meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Millions Are To Be Grabbed Out Here, and Your Only Competition Is Idiots'?
meta.ogDescription: A real telegram, almost certainly. Its sole source is Ben Hecht’s memoir, and even the year is disputed: 1925 or 1926.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1897–1953 · American screenwriter, co-author of Citizen Kane
answer.sourceLine: Mankiewicz sent it as a telegram to Ben Hecht, luring him from Broadway to Paramount, and the full text runs: “Will you accept three hundred per week to work for Paramount Pictures. All expenses paid. The three hundred is peanuts. Millions are to be grabbed out here and your only competition is idiots. Don’t let this get around.” The catch is the evidence. Quote Investigator finds the only primary record in Hecht’s own 1954 memoir ↗, A Child of the Century — and Mankiewicz had died in March 1953, a year before it was published. The wire itself is not known to survive. As QI puts it, “the accuracy of the colorful text appears to depend on the veracity of Hecht”, who was a magnificent storyteller by trade. Even the date is unsettled: Hecht says spring 1925, while later scholarship and Wikipedia both say 1926.

source.excerpt: The telegram he delivered on this spring day in 1925 came from the unknown Scythian wastes of Hollywood, Calif. It read, “Will you accept three hundred per week to work for Paramount Pictures. All expenses paid. The three hundred is peanuts. Millions are to be grabbed out here and your only competition is idiots. Don’t let this get around.” — “Herman Mankiewicz.”
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ gives the full telegram and names its primary evidence: A Child of the Century by Ben Hecht, 1954, Simon and Schuster, New York, quote page 466, marked “Verified with scans”. QI’s conclusion is quoted in full on this page rather than paraphrased, because the hedge is the finding.

QI also documents the line escaping into print almost immediately. A review of Hecht’s memoir — Van Allen Bradley, “Turbulent Autobiography: Ben Hecht’s Book Is Gay, Bitter, Vulgar”, The Sunday Press (Binghamton, New York), 27 June 1954, page 10-B, column 2 — reprinted the two sentences and attributed them vaguely to “a film magnate”, not to Mankiewicz by name.

The second retelling QI cites is Mark Jacobson, “New York You Oughta Be in Pictures”, New York Magazine, 29 December 1975, quote page 36, which prints the wire in capitals and dates it 1925 — following Hecht.

Wikiquote’s Mankiewicz page ↗ carries the telegram but dates it 1926, citing Julien Gorbach, The Notorious Ben Hecht: Iconoclastic Writer and Militant Zionist (Purdue University Press, 2019), page 92. That citation is reported here as Wikiquote gives it; the Gorbach book was not consulted directly.

Wikipedia’s article on Hecht ↗ also puts the telegram in 1926, and its article on Mankiewicz ↗ has him working as assistant theater editor at The New York Times from 1923 to 1926 and moving to Hollywood around 1926, on a Paramount salary of $400 a week. Those dates and Hecht’s “spring 1925” cannot both be right; this page therefore reports the conflict instead of resolving it.
source.excerptNote: Hecht’s own framing, as transcribed by Quote Investigator from the 1954 book ↗. Note that the famous sentence is the fourth of five, and the funniest line may be the last one: having described a gold rush, Mankiewicz asks Hecht to keep it quiet. The boldface marks the portion that travelled.

The telegram was a private message, never published at the time, and the only text of it reaches us through Ben Hecht’s A Child of the Century, copyright 1954 — well after the 1931 public-domain cutoff. Mankiewicz died in 1953, but a private wire is not made public domain by its sender’s death, and no one has produced the original. Quoted here briefly for comment and criticism.

author.name: Herman J. Mankiewicz
author.heading: About Herman J. Mankiewicz
author.metaLine: 1897–1953 · American screenwriter, co-author of Citizen Kane
author.bio: Herman Jacob Mankiewicz (7 November 1897 – 5 March 1953) was an American journalist turned screenwriter. He was assistant theater editor at The New York Times from 1923 to 1926 and The New Yorker’s first regular theatre critic, before going to Hollywood and ending 1927 as head of Paramount’s scenario department. He co-wrote Citizen Kane (1941) with Orson Welles and shared the Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay for it; his other credits include Dinner at Eight and The Pride of the Yankees, and he contributed to The Wizard of Oz. He died in Los Angeles at 55 of uremic poisoning brought on by liver failure.

misattribution.heading: What to watch for
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is credited with this one — it is Mankiewicz’s in every retelling. The problems are of a different kind: a single witness, a contested year, and a wording that is usually cut down to its best half.

items.who: Ben Hecht, the recipient and the only witness
items.why: Everything known about this telegram comes from the man it was sent to, writing roughly three decades later, after the sender was dead. QI says so plainly ↗: “the accuracy of the colorful text appears to depend on the veracity of Hecht”, and it does not know whether the wire survives in any collection. Hecht was a screenwriter and a memoirist with a well-earned reputation for improving a story.

Hecht dates it to “this spring day in 1925” and New York Magazine followed him in 1975. But Wikiquote dates it 1926 on Gorbach’s authority ↗, Wikipedia’s Hecht article says 1926 ↗, and Hecht’s first screen credit, Underworld, is 1927. Treat any single year you see attached to this telegram as unsettled.

What gets quoted is “millions are to be grabbed out here and your only competition is idiots” — usually without “Don’t let this get around”, which is the joke, and without the salary offer that makes it a job pitch rather than an aphorism. Transcriptions also wobble: Wikiquote’s has “three hundred dollars per week to work for Paramount?” where Hecht has “three hundred per week to work for Paramount Pictures.”

misattribution.truthLine: QI’s verdict ↗: the telegram is documented only in Hecht’s 1954 memoir, so its accuracy rests on Hecht. Nothing contradicts it, and nothing independently confirms it — which is why this page says attributed and not verified.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In the mid-1920s the serious writers were in New York and the money was in California, and the two facts were felt as an insult. Mankiewicz — a Berlin correspondent turned theatre editor turned New Yorker critic — had gone west and was cheerfully reporting back that the industry was rich and the competition was weak. The telegram is the whole Broadway-versus-Hollywood attitude of the decade compressed into five sentences, which is exactly why historians keep reaching for it.

It also worked. Hecht went, wrote Underworld, and won the first Academy Award for Best Original Story in 1929 for it. He spent the rest of his life being well paid for films he publicly despised — the same memoir that preserves this telegram calls the movies “an eruption of trash that has lamed the American mind”. Mankiewicz, for his part, got to the top of Paramount’s scenario department and then to Citizen Kane, and died at 55.
detailsBody: The date problem is worth sitting with, because it is the kind of thing that gets quietly smoothed over. Hecht’s memoir says the messenger arrived on a spring day in 1925. Wikipedia’s account of Mankiewicz has him as assistant theater editor at The New York Times from 1923 to 1926, writing The New Yorker’s theatre column during 1925 and early 1926, and moving to Hollywood around 1926 after Walter Wanger offered him a contract. A telegram sent from “the unknown Scythian wastes of Hollywood” in spring 1925 does not fit that chronology. This page does not pick a winner, because no source consulted here reconciles them; it just declines to print one year as a fact.

The other honest gap: Quote Investigator says it does not know whether the physical telegram is held in any memorabilia collection. If it is, this page is wrong to hedge and should be corrected. Until then, a line that every Hollywood history quotes rests on one man’s recollection of a piece of paper nobody can produce.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI gives the telegram in full as 'Will you accept three hundred per week to work for Paramount Pictures. All expenses paid. The three hundred is peanuts. Millions are to be grabbed out here and your only competition is idiots. Don't let this get around. Herman Mankiewicz.' and names its primary evidence as Ben Hecht, A Child of the Century, 1954, Simon and Schuster, quote page 466, verified with scans.

QI concludes 'the accuracy of the colorful text appears to depend on the veracity of Hecht' and states it does not know if the telegram itself is held in a memorabilia collection; it notes Mankiewicz died a year before Hecht's book was published.

QI cites a 27 June 1954 review by Van Allen Bradley in The Sunday Press (Binghamton, New York), quote page 10-B column 2, which reprints the two sentences and credits 'a film magnate'; and Mark Jacobson, 'New York You Oughta Be in Pictures', New York Magazine, 29 December 1975, quote page 36, which dates the telegram 1925.

Wikiquote's Herman J. Mankiewicz page carries the telegram dated 1926, cited to Julien Gorbach, The Notorious Ben Hecht: Iconoclastic Writer and Militant Zionist (West Lafayette, Indiana: Purdue University Press, 2019), p. 92.

Herman J. Mankiewicz was born 7 November 1897 and died 5 March 1953 in Los Angeles at 55 of uremic poisoning due to liver failure; he was assistant theater editor at The New York Times 1923-1926, The New Yorker's first regular theatre critic, head of Paramount's scenario department by the end of 1927, and shared the Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay for Citizen Kane.

Wikipedia's Ben Hecht article dates the Mankiewicz telegram to 1926, quotes its text, gives Hecht's dates as 28 February 1894 - 18 April 1964, and names Underworld (1927) as his first screenplay, for which he won an Academy Award at the first ceremony.
The Internet Archive holds a copy of A Child of the Century by Ben Hecht; the catalogued copy is a New American Library printing dated 1954.

Wikipedia's Underworld (1927 film) article states 'Ben Hecht won the Academy Award for Writing in the 1st Academy Awards ceremony in 1929 for his work on this film' and 'Ben Hecht won an Academy Award for Best Original Story'.
